newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian ruling party members urge new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian ruling party members urge new cabinet.

text.p: Leading members of Bulgaria's governing Socialist party have called for formation of a new cabinet and wide-ranging policy reforms following the party's decisive defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
An open letter to the Socialist leadership and parliamentary group published in the party daily Douma on Tuesday called for urgent action to ensure the party completed its parliamentary term.
The letter called for formation of a new cabinet "with prestigious and experienced people from the relevant sectors".

"Special attention should be paid to gather a strong economic team of people who are experienced in the real economy, finance, new technology, agriculture, and science," said the letter signed by 19 senior Socialists.

Preliminary results from Sunday's run-off give pro-market liberal Petar Stoyanov of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) 60 percent of the vote to Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov's 40 percent.

Although the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament, where the Socialists have a majority, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said the party must take note of the electorate's strong message of disapproval.

The letter called for a structural reform plan, measures to restore agricultural output and avert food shortages, initiatives to stabilise the banking system and secure foreign funding and measures to restore political dialogue.
Once these steps had been taken, an extraordinary congress should be held to stabilise the party's position as the governing power in Bulgaria, it said.

"These seven proposals are not a full programme for continuation of the parliamentary mandate but, in our view, they are actions without which we may face a dramatic situation. This is why we are suggesting their urgent discussion and adoption," the letter said.

Videnov, who is also leader of the party set up by ex-communists after former leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, said a party congress could be held as early as January to review policy and did not rule out cabinet changes.
The party's supreme council will meet this week, then a leadership plenum is set for November 11.
The letter said there had been a sharp fall in public confidence in the government, whose approval rating had fallen to 10 to 15 percent now from 49 to 55 percent in spring 1995.
But it did not mention Videnov, who is often criticised for his secretive and authoritarian style and has presided over a growing economic crisis.

The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar at the start of the year to 249 on Tuesday. Annual inflation is forecast at 240 percent and many Bulgarians say they are having to choose between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
An International Monetary Fund mission is in Sofia discussing terms for release of a $115 million credit vital to avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

The funds have twice been delayed because of the government's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.

"This is the BSP's last chance to take the initiative on decisions which will allow it to keep its parliamentary mandate for governing the country," said the letter. Parliament was elected in December 1994 for a four-year term.

Signatories of the letter included respected former party chairman Alexander Lilov, deputy chairman Yanaki Stoilov and other prominent party members, many of them from the reformist Union for Social Democracy wing.
